label: Configuration Space
notes: This chapter spans printed pages eleven through fifty-eight and asks one question: how do joints, loops, and constraints turn a physical mechanism into a geometric space. We treat configuration as a point on a curved manifold, and degrees of freedom as the dimension of that manifold rather than a list of angles.

label: Configuration and Degrees of Freedom
notes: A configuration is the complete specification of every point of the robot, captured as a single point of the configuration space. The number of degrees of freedom equals the dimension of that space: the smallest count of real parameters needed to pin the mechanism down completely and unambiguously.

label: Counting by Subtraction
notes: The summation principle counts freedoms by starting from all rigid bodies moving independently, then subtracting the constraints imposed by every joint. Each joint of a given type removes a fixed number of relative freedoms, so degrees of freedom equal total body freedoms minus total joint constraints across the mechanism.

label: Joint Types and Their Freedoms
notes: Joints differ by how many relative freedoms they permit. A revolute or prismatic joint grants one, a cylindrical two, a spherical three. In the plane each joint type allows fewer freedoms than in space, so the same hardware constrains differently depending on whether motion is planar or spatial.

label: Grubler's Formula
notes: Grubler's formula packages the summation principle for mechanisms with one ground link. Degrees of freedom equal m times links-minus-joints-minus-one plus the sum of joint freedoms, where m is six for spatial and three for planar mechanisms. Ground and the loop closures are handled automatically by the count.

label: Worked Count: Four-Bar Linkage
notes: The planar four-bar linkage has four links including ground and four revolute joints. With m equal to three, Grubler gives three times four minus four minus one, plus four, which equals one. A single freedom drives the whole closed loop, matching the crank we turn by hand.

label: Topology of the C-Space
notes: Configuration spaces have an intrinsic shape independent of coordinates. A single revolute joint traces a circle, a spherical wrist sweeps a two-sphere, and two stacked revolute joints fill a torus. This topology is fixed by the mechanism; no choice of numbers can change a circle into a flat line.

label: The 2R Arm Torus
notes: A two revolute arm has two angles, each living on its own circle, so its configuration space is the product of two circles, the torus. The flat angle square is only a chart: its left and right edges are the same points, and its top and bottom edges glue together as well.

label: Explicit versus Implicit
notes: A space can be described two ways. An explicit parametrization names a few coordinates and maps them onto the space, like joint angles for an arm. An implicit description writes constraint equations whose solution set is the space, like the unit-norm equation that carves a sphere out of three-dimensional coordinates.

label: Rigid-Body Configuration: SE(3)
notes: The configuration of a free rigid body in space needs three numbers for position and three for orientation, giving six degrees of freedom. These configurations form the special Euclidean group, a six dimensional manifold. In the plane the analog is three dimensional, with two translations and one rotation angle.

label: Holonomic versus Nonholonomic
notes: Holonomic constraints are equations on configuration alone; they cut the dimension of the space and can be integrated. Nonholonomic constraints restrict velocities through Pfaffian forms that cannot be integrated into configuration equations. Rolling without slipping is the classic case: it limits motion directions yet still reaches every configuration.

label: Task Space and Workspace
notes: Task space is the space in which the robot's task is naturally expressed, often end-effector poses. The workspace is the set of configurations the end-effector can actually reach. Both are projections of the configuration space, useful pictures that must not be mistaken for the full C-space.
